title: Greedy Best-First finds the fastest vibes in Hobart!
description: Watch Greedy Best-First race across a real street-graph of Hobart, always expanding the node that looks closest to the goal. It’s fast, heuristic-driven pathfinding—perfect for visual intuition about how informed search behaves on maps.
ig_caption:
🗺️✨ Hobart streets, mapped as a graph—then solved with **Greedy Best-First**! 

In this visualization, each intersection is a node and each road segment is an edge (weighted using approximate distances). Greedy Best-First selects the next expansion by minimizing the **heuristic h(n)**—typically straight-line distance to the destination (often computed from coordinates). 

📌 Key idea (graph theory): it performs **informed graph search** by using a priority queue ordered by **h(n)**, not by the true accumulated cost from the start (**g(n)**). That means it can reach the goal quickly, but it’s not guaranteed to find the globally shortest path when heuristics mislead it—especially around detours and road geometry. 

✅ Want to see how it compares to A* or Dijkstra on the same map? Drop a comment with “A* vs Greedy” and I’ll make the next reel! 💬🚀
fb_caption:
Hobart (Battery Point) becomes a real street-graph 🗺️—and **Greedy Best-First** explores it using only a heuristic estimate to the goal. In graph search terms, every intersection is a node, roads are edges, and the algorithm repeatedly expands the most “promising” frontier node based on **h(n)** (often straight-line distance). 

Because it doesn’t account for total traveled cost (**g(n)**), Greedy can be blazing fast but may miss the absolute shortest route. Like, share, and follow for more real-map algorithm visualizations!
yt_description:
🏁 Hobart street map pathfinding with **Greedy Best-First**! 
In this YouTube Shorts, we convert real roads into a graph (nodes=intersections, edges=road segments) and run **Greedy Best-First** using a heuristic (straight-line distance) to always choose the next closest-looking node. 

⚙️ Mechanics: priority queue ordered by h(n), heuristic-only decision-making, fast progress but no guarantee of shortest path.
